n: The wall is nearly done — every gap closed, though the gate doors are not yet hung. With mockery and threats failing, the enemies change tactics again.

f.g: No gaps remaining in the wall.

n: Sanballat and Geshem invite Nehemiah to a “friendly” meeting in the plain of Ono, about 25 miles away near the coast. It was a trap to harm him.

f.g: A valley northwest of Jerusalem near modern Tel Aviv, on the edge of Judah’s territory.

n: Nehemiah’s famous answer: I am doing a great work and cannot come down. He refuses to be distracted from what God has asked him to do.

f.w: I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down

n: They ask four times; he gives the same answer four times. Persistence in temptation is met with persistence in purpose.
The fifth message is an unsealed letter — meant to be read by others along the way and to spread the rumor.

f.g: An unsealed letter, so its accusations would become public gossip.

n: The letter claims Nehemiah is building the wall to rebel and make himself king. This was a dangerous charge in the Persian Empire and had stopped the work once before.

f.g: Another form of the name Geshem.

n: It even claims he has hired prophets to proclaim him king. The threat is clear: meet with us, or we will report this to Artaxerxes.

f.w: There is a king in Judah
f.g: Hopes for a restored Davidic king were real, which made the rumor believable.

n: Nehemiah flatly denies it: you made this up. He doesn’t waste time defending himself at length.

f.w: thou feignest them out of thine own heart
f.g: You are inventing these things yourself.

n: Nehemiah sees the real goal: to frighten the builders so they would quit. His response is a short prayer — “O God, strengthen my hands.”
Now a fellow Jew, Shemaiah, who claims to have a prophecy, urges Nehemiah to hide inside the temple because assassins are coming.

f.g: Confined to his house — perhaps pretending to be in danger, or in a ritual state.
The holy place, where only priests were allowed (Numbers 18:7).

n: Nehemiah refuses. A leader running to hide would discourage the people, and as a layman he had no right to enter the temple’s holy place.

f.w: Should such a man as I flee?
f.g: A governor fleeing would shatter the people’s courage.

n: Nehemiah discerns that this “prophecy” was not from God — Shemaiah had been bribed by the enemies. Spiritual discernment protected him.
The plan was to scare Nehemiah into sinning so he would lose credibility. Enemies often try to destroy a leader’s reputation when they can’t stop the work.
Nehemiah again leaves justice to God. He names a false prophetess, Noadiah, and others who joined the scheme to frighten him.

f.g: Mentioned only here; one of several false prophets working against Nehemiah.

n: The wall is finished in only fifty-two days — an astonishing speed, achieved through unity, hard work, and God’s help.

f.g: The sixth month, roughly August–September, 445 BC.
About seven and a half weeks.

n: The surrounding nations lose heart, recognizing that this work was done with God’s help. The finished wall became a witness of God’s power.

f.w: cast down in their own eyes
this work was wrought of our God

n: An inside problem remains: some nobles of Judah were secretly in steady contact with Tobiah.
Tobiah had married into a leading Jewish family, and his son married the daughter of Meshullam, one of the wall’s builders. These marriage ties gave him loyal allies inside Jerusalem.

f.g: Bound to him by oath or alliance.

n: These nobles praised Tobiah to Nehemiah and passed Nehemiah’s words back to Tobiah, while Tobiah kept sending threatening letters. Divided loyalties among God’s people can be as dangerous as outside enemies.

f.g: Reported what I said to him — acting as informants.
